Shortbelly rockfish (Sebastes jordani) attains an ultimate total length of 32 centimeters [Li = 32 centimeters], a size that positions this species among the smaller members of the genus Sebastes, whose larger congeners can exceed 80 centimeters. This maximum recorded length is derived from extensive trawl surveys conducted along the continental slope of California and Oregon, where the species is most abundant at depths between 100 and 300 meters. The mass of a fully grown adult has been estimated from length-weight regressions fitted to thousands of specimens, yielding an ultimate wet weight of 193 grams [Wwi = 193 grams], a value consistent with the fusiform body plan that facilitates efficient midwater foraging on zooplankton. Field observations indicate that growth in this species proceeds slowly after the onset of maturity, with length increments diminishing considerably once individuals approach this asymptotic size. The relatively modest maximum size of Shortbelly rockfish reflects a life-history strategy that prioritizes early reproductive output over continued somatic expansion, an adaptive response to the high natural mortality rates characteristic of pelagic environments.

Puberty in Shortbelly rockfish occurs at a total length of 14 centimeters [Lp = 14 centimeters], a developmental milestone that marks the transition from the juvenile to the adult phase. At this size, individuals have accumulated sufficient somatic reserves to support the energetic demands of gonadal maturation, and their wet weight at puberty is approximately 14.7 grams [Wwp = approximately 14.7 grams], derived from the same length-mass scaling relationship used to estimate adult mass. This relatively early onset of reproductive capability, compared to the species' maximum size, is a defining feature of its opportunistic life history, allowing young adults to contribute to the next generation before encountering the elevated predation pressures that accompany larger body sizes in the water column. Histological examinations of gonadal tissue confirm that primary oocyte development and spermatogenesis are initiated at this length threshold, with the first spawning typically occurring within the same calendar year that puberty is attained. The modest body mass at this stage highlights the energetic trade-off between continued growth and the initiation of reproductive investment.

Reproductive output in Shortbelly rockfish peaks under the thermal conditions characteristic of its deep-water habitat, approximately 8.2 °C [T = 8.2 °C]. At this temperature, females produce an average of 75,000 larvae per spawning event [N_R_i = 75,000 larvae per spawning event], a figure that reflects the species' viviparous mode of reproduction and its reliance on a single, annual spawning event [F_R_i = single, annual spawning event], which translates to a daily reproductive rate of approximately 205 larvae per day [Ri = approximately 205 larvae per day]. The individual larvae themselves are modest in size, with each newly released larva possessing a minute wet weight of 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams], a value consistent with the small egg diameter of 0.8 millimeters from which they develop internally and among the lowest recorded for the genus Sebastes, highlighting the extreme fecundity required to offset high larval mortality. The relatively cool temperature of 8.2 °C [T = 8.2 °C] appears to optimize the balance between maternal metabolic costs and the developmental rate of embryos within the ovary, as inferred from laboratory-maintained gravid females.

The lifespan of Shortbelly rockfish is known to be exceptionally long for a fish of its body size, with the maximum recorded longevity reaching 31 years [am = 31 years] when assessed at the species' typical ambient temperature of 8.2 °C [T = 8.2 °C]. This remarkable longevity is derived from otolith age validation studies that have examined annuli from individuals collected across the species' geographic range, with the oldest specimens recovered from the colder, deeper portions of the continental slope. The age structure of wild populations shows a gradual accumulation of older age classes, a pattern that is consistent with the low natural mortality rates that allow individuals to survive for decades in the absence of intense fishing pressure. When expressed in terms of total days, this maximum lifespan corresponds to approximately 11,315 days [am = approximately 11,315 days] of life under the same thermal regime, a duration that is notable among small-bod at a temperature of 8.2 °C [T = 8.2 °C]ied rockfishes. Comparative analyses within the genus Sebastes suggest that the exceptional longevity of Shortbelly rockfish may be linked to its slow metabolic rate at depth, a physiological adaptation that reduces oxidative damage over time.

A synoptic view of the life history of Shortbelly rockfish reveals a suite of traits finely tuned to the stable but food-limited environment of the continental slope. The moderate asymptotic length of 32 centimeters [Li = 32 centimeters] is accompanied by a wet weight at puberty of 14.7 grams [Wwp = 14.7 grams], representing about 7.6 percent of the adult mass of 193 grams [Wwi = 193 grams], indicating that reproductive investment begins at a relatively small body size. The extreme fecundity of 75,000 larvae per spawning event [N_R_i = 75,000 larvae per spawning event] combined with the single annual reproductive cycle [F_R_i = single annual reproductive cycle] yields a daily output of approximately 205 larvae [Ri = daily output of approximately 205 larvae] over the extended lifespan of more than three decades (31 years) [am = 31 years], all under the prevailing thermal conditions of 8.2 °C [T = 8.2 °C]. The minute size of each newborn larva at 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams] imposes a high initial mortality risk, but the sheer number of progeny ensures that some recruits survive to exploit the deep scattering layer's zooplankton resources. This combination of life-history traits places Shortbelly rockfish among the more extreme K-selected strategists within the mesopelagic fish assemblage.
